Industry News: How This Creepy Critter Evolved Its Way to Surviving on Blood Alone

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Misunderstood and often maligned, vampire bats are saddled with a reputation akin to that of Nosferatu and Dracula just because they feed on blood.
  • Because vampire bats only feed on blood, they’re the only obligate sanguivores among mammals and, in fact, among all tetrapods—since their wings are modified forelimbs, they still count as four-limbed animals.
  • It has been revealed that evolutionary genomicist Michael Hiller of the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, wanted to learn how these fascinating creatures are genetically programmed to live on blood alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Misunderstood and often maligned, vampire bats are saddled with a reputation akin to that of Nosferatu and Dracula just because they feed on blood. But unlike the vampires of movies and folklore, they don’t drain their victims. These tiny creatures couldn’t possibly hold all the blood that’s inside the much larger mammals they feed on after dark. Still, they can still consume a seemingly supernatural amount because their stomachs are built to expand.

Because vampire bats only feed on blood, they’re the only obligate sanguivores among mammals and, in fact, among all tetrapods—since their wings are modified forelimbs, they still count as four-limbed animals. When night falls, they fly out to forage, sometimes drinking up to half their own body weight in blood, thanks to those expandable stomachs and kidneys that quickly get rid of excess fluid. The problem is that blood is a poor diet. It’s mostly water, with plenty of protein but potentially toxic levels of iron, and only traces of sugar and fat. Even so, it’s the only food vampire bats will ever know. Once the young of all three living species are weaned off milk, they switch entirely to blood. They start sinking their teeth into unsuspecting victims, mostly sleeping livestock, which feel little more than a mosquito bite.

It has been revealed that evolutionary genomicist Michael Hiller of the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, wanted to learn how these fascinating creatures are genetically programmed to live on blood alone. He and his research team set out to identify the changes in genes and gene expression that made this possible. They analyzed the genomes of the common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus), the hairy-legged vampire bat (Diphylla ecaudata) and the white-winged vampire bat (Diaemus youngi), and compared them with the genomes of other bat species. By analyzing gene expression in six major organs, including the stomach, they found several anomalies. Vampire bats’ stomachs were so different from those of other bats, and other animals, that they were almost a different organ entirely.

In a recent development, “Extreme dietary specializations impose strong and persistent selective pressures in nature, forcing organisms to reconcile severe nutritional imbalances with existing physiological and metabolic constraints,” Hiller and his colleagues wrote in a study recently posted to the preprint server bioRxiv. “Deciphering how genomes adapt to such conditions reveals general principles of the evolutionary processes that remodel metabolism and physiology.”.

Sources indicate that among the roughly 30,000 known tetrapod species, dependence on blood, known as obligate sanguivory, has evolved only once. Because blood offers so few calories for its volume, vampire bats have to drink large amounts of it. Because it also contains so little sugar, the bats have low baseline insulin levels and release little insulin after a meal. Some aspects of this metabolic situation resemble type 2 diabetes in humans, so studying these bats could lead to better treatments in the future. Much like fictional vampires, vampire bats also need to feed often. They have a very limited ability to store fat and glycogen, so they can starve if they go 48 to 72 hours without a blood meal. To prevent this, bats that have fed successfully sometimes regurgitate blood for roost mates that haven’t eaten that night.

Recent findings suggest that the genomic shifts behind vampire bats’ sanguivory include changes in genes for digestion, metabolism and immunity, as well as the loss of bitter taste receptors. The vampire bat stomach in particular has adaptations found only in these three species. Its enlarged size is linked to three upregulated genes. These genes are also thought to play a role in the bats’ unusually shaped gastric glands and in extra connective tissue that makes such huge expansion possible. Most mammals use stomach acid to digest food, but vampire bats’ genes for producing gastric acid are suppressed. Digesting so much blood would take an enormous amount of acid, and the specialized mucus lining their stomachs leaves them vulnerable to acid damage. So over the course of their evolution, their stomachs shifted from digesting food to absorbing it.

Industry observers note that adaptations elsewhere in the body also help these winged vampires survive on their unusual diet. Insect-eating bats have an enzyme for digesting insect sugars that their vampire relatives lack. Vampire bats get hardly any sugar, so they have no need for it, which fits with their low insulin output. Vampire bats have also lost several genes that control gut movement in other species, but that matters little for an animal whose diet is a single liquid with little, if any, indigestible material. Similarly, having fewer fat-digesting enzymes is no disadvantage, since blood contains hardly any fat. Meanwhile, genes for coping with blood’s excess iron are enhanced. Vampire bats also rely more on their intestines to absorb amino acids and on their kidneys to reabsorb them, which keeps amino acids from being lost in urine.

According to recent reports, studying genomes and gene expression across several organs together was key to these findings. “This integrative approach was essential for obtaining a comprehensive view of the molecular changes associated with sanguivory in vampire bats,” Hiller noted. “More generally, our work demonstrates how genome-wide, integrative analyses can yield molecular insights into the evolution of adaptive traits.”.

The 7 Best Portable Jump Starters to Bring Your Vehicle Back to Life

📅 23 Nov 2021 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help.
  • A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

In a recent development, like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also important to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

There are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In a recent development, in short, each device in this roundup can promptly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

My recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

According to recent reports, with 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

This device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts.

The GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—key so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

In a recent development, protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

Sources indicate that the interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review.

Recent findings suggest that this is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

It has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

Sources indicate that like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

In a recent development, the Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

Full Noco GB40 Boost Plus Review.

Recent findings suggest that if you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.).

Industry observers note that I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so users need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

For motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

This device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

Industry observers note that with 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

Industry observers note that for years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

According to recent reports, with 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

Recent findings suggest that this portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Industry observers note that something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

The Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

According to recent reports, portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

The two most vital specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Industry observers note that bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

It has been revealed that portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against challenges like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

In a recent development, most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

If you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

According to recent reports, look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

In a recent development, A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

Yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two important. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

Definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will glitch a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

According to recent reports, yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That remarked, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

Sources indicate that isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

Sources indicate that to piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Industry observers note that most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard.

A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

Sources indicate that if you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

It has been revealed that full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST on November 24, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon. A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars.

Sources indicate that this is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so massive and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

It has been revealed that the 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed promptly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 23, 1221, Alfonso X was born in Spain, the son of King Ferdinand III of Castile and Leon. By the time he succeeded his father in 1252, Alfonso was already known as a scholar – though he demonstrated his military might as well, putting down several revolts and annexing Murcia.

Known as Alfonso the Wise, the king pioneered efforts to translate Arabic and Andalusian works of astronomy into the vernacular Castilian. His multicultural court authored scholarly works and engineered scientific instruments, as well as collecting an extensive library of works on astrology and astronomy. Alfonso also commissioned the Alfosine Tables, astronomical tables based on Arabic sources and updated with new observations – facilitated by new astronomical instruments constructed at Alfonso’s orders. The work included stellar and planetary positions and became the standard for astronomy in Europe for the late medieval and early Renaissance periods.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.
  • Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” indicates geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

Recent findings suggest that that tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

In a recent development, as for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern indicates. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Sources indicate that instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a fresh version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

It has been revealed that the discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”.

It has been revealed that A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The brain is a wondrous organ that’s so complex it’s often referred to as a computer, complete with electrical wiring in the forms of neurons, synapses, and axons. However, unlike computers, there’s no easy way to deftly repair faulty wiring, especially down at the cellular level. For decades, the best tools at a physician's disposal for tackling serious neurological diseases were medications or, in more dire scenarios, external therapies such as deep brain stimulation.

Those treatments can bring real relief, but they don’t fix the underlying problem. But if the brain really runs on electrical connections, shouldn’t it be possible to route signals around damaged areas by rewiring specific neurons? A team of U.S. researchers led by Kafui Dzirasa of Duke University School of Medicine thinks so. In May, they described a fresh technology called “LinCx” in the journal Nature. It uses engineered versions of proteins found in fish that naturally form electrical synapses, and it can link two specifically chosen neurons.

Sources indicate that “For decades, neuroscience has lacked tools that can precisely control communication between specific cell types,” Dzirasa, the senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “By introducing a way to plug in new electrical connections with cellular‑level precision, our study marks a major step forward in the ability to edit brain circuitry and understand how neural networks give rise to behavior.”.

The system relies on structures called “gap junctions.” Each one is made of two hemichannels, and each hemichannel is built from six proteins called connexins. Through these gap junctions, cells exchange chemical and electrical signals, but they usually form unpredictably across cells. The innovation of the LinCx system is that it uses modified proteins that dock with one another while ignoring native brain proteins.

“The goal sounded almost simple: Make two proteins connect only to each other,” Carnegie Mellon’s Elizabeth Ransey, former Duke University postdoctoral researcher and lead author, mentioned in a separate press statement. “We can specify both sides of the connection. That gives us much more precision than approaches that activate one population and indirectly affect everything downstream.”.

The team tested the system in simple structures, such as human-derived cells and frog oocytes, and eventually moved on to more complex ones. Previous studies have rewired the neural circuits of Caenorhabditis elegans, a species of nematode commonly used in neurobiology. However, using the technology on mammals, specifically laboratory mice, was a first. In both worms and mice, the scientists noted changing behavior after performing this “neural bypass.” C. elegans, for example, modified its temperature-seeking behavior, and mice altered targeted responses to social interaction and stress.

By focusing on bypassing damaged areas rather than repairing them, physicians could provide improved brain function in those experiencing depression, autism, and many types of neurodegenerative disease.

The amazing Crab Nebula

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one of my personal favorite objects in the night sky is the Crab Nebula (M1).
  • Industry observers note that the Crab Nebula burst onto the scene in 1054 C.E., when a massive star in the constellation Taurus collapsed in on itself in a supernova whose light was visible during the day, as documented by multiple civilizations around the world.
  • Industry observers note that pulsars are some of the most extreme objects in the universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one of my personal favorite objects in the night sky is the Crab Nebula (M1). It’s No. 1 on Charles Messier’s list, although I don’t think he ordered his objects by how cool they are (a missed opportunity!). It’s not exactly impressive visually in most scopes — mostly a gray blob, or a spiky gray blob in larger apertures — but it’s one of those targets that if you know what you are looking at, it becomes immensely more interesting to observe.

Industry observers note that the Crab Nebula burst onto the scene in 1054 C.E., when a massive star in the constellation Taurus collapsed in on itself in a supernova whose light was visible during the day, as documented by multiple civilizations around the world. Its leftover shell of gas and dust has been expanding ever since, and the bright glow is still visible thanks to what remains of the progenitor star: a rapidly spinning neutron star, known as a pulsar. The “crab” moniker stems from a drawing made by the William Parsons, Earl of Rosse, in the early 1840s with a 36-inch telescope, which depicts crab-leg-like appendages, although he later noted that observations through a 72-inch resulted in a view that looked rather different than his original drawing.

Industry observers note that pulsars are some of the most extreme objects in the universe. The Crab Pulsar, which is approximately 12–17 miles (20–28 kilometers) in diameter, spins at a breakneck 30 times per second — once every 33 milliseconds. At magnitude 16.6, it is a very difficult catch, but possible in large (20-plus-inch) scopes on nights with steady skies. It sits only a few arcseconds from a slightly brighter magnitude 15.8 star that guides the way. The pulsar produces a relativistic-speed stellar wind that generates synchrotron radiation, which occurs when charged particles move along curved paths, bent by strong magnetic fields. This is seen across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio to gamma rays, forming the main diffuse part of the nebula’s emission. This radiation has a total luminosity some 100,000 times greater than the Sun’s! The pulsar is slowing down gradually as a result of energy carried away by its stellar wind, increasing its period by 36 nanoseconds per day.

Recent findings suggest that the nebula is still expanding, even nearly 1,000 years later, at a rate of 3.4 million mph (5.5 million km/h) — that’s 950 miles (1,527 km) per second, or 0.5% the speed of light! While not noticeable in a single observation, comparing images across several years highlights the expansion on very human-accessible timescales.

According to recent reports, the Crab’s intricate filaments are what make it so visually stunning in images. These structures are the remnants of the star’s atmosphere, consisting of gases like ionized helium, hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, iron, neon, and sulfur. It’s a moderately tricky astrophotography target to process: In wideband, it has a largely gray interior wrapped in red tendrils, so it is best imaged in narrowband, where it can display incredible, intricate detail that looks well and truly alien. A famous colorful 2005 Hubble image uses narrowband light from oxygen and sulfur and has oxygen-III set as red, sulfur-II as green, and oxygen-I as blue. When I’ve shot the Crab, I used hydrogen-alpha as blue, since it is a similar wavelength to oxygen-I (which are both red in reality) to create an image reminiscent of the Hubble one, much to my delight.

In a recent development, whether you are a primarily visual astronomer or a high-tech shutterbug like me, the Crab Nebula is worth spending a little time with this month. Take a moment during your observing to realize how incredible this object is. Rising in the evening hours, it will be up all night for you to enjoy. How much detail can you tease out? Can you spot the pulsar?

Molly Wakeling is an avid astrophotographer active in STEM outreach. She has a Ph.D. in nuclear engineering.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

According to recent reports, rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

Sources indicate that “Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”.

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, stated she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses unveiled a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

Industry observers note that the two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack stated she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”.

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”.

Leger Fernández mentioned if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández remarked. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”.

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, Roscosmos is targeting 5:13 a.m. EST to launch the Progress MS-36 cargo ship to the International Space Station (ISS) on a Soyuz-2.1b from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, according to Next Spaceflight. NASA still lists the flight only as no earlier than fall 2026 and has not given a date.

In a recent development, at 5:45 a.m. EST, Arianespace will try again to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 Amazon Leo satellites. A problem with the rocket’s ground support systems halted Monday’s countdown. It is Amazon’s first launch since last week’s Vulcan failure.

Later that morning, at 10:55 a.m. EST, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has stated what the rocket carries. The booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

According to recent reports, that evening, at 7:18 p.m. EST, a Long March 2F is slated to launch Shenzhou-24, carrying three astronauts, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China to the Tiangong space station, per Next Spaceflight.

One seat makes history. A Pakistani astronaut will fly as a payload specialist, becoming the first foreign visitor to Tiangong and Pakistan’s first astronaut. Pakistan’s space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), has shortlisted two pilots, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. One will fly and the other will serve as backup. The astronaut is expected to spend about a week on Tiangong and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

According to recent reports, on Thursday, Nov. 26, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 4:35 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been declared.

Sources indicate that later Thursday, at 7:05 p.m. EST, Rocket Lab will launch Night Owls Never Sleep on an Electron from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula.The payload is a StriX satellite for the Japanese manufacturer Synspective. StriX satellites use synthetic aperture radar to image the ground through clouds and darkness.

Recent findings suggest that on Friday, Nov. 27, CASC is targeting 8:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 6A launch from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been unveiled.

On Saturday, Nov. 28, CAS Space, a commercial launch tech giant backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, aims to launch a Kinetica 1 at 8:00 p.m. EST from a sea platform in the South China Sea, supported by the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport, per Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been confirmed.

Industry observers note that later Saturday, at 10:50 p.m. EST, a Long March 6C is slated to lift off from Taiyuan, according to Next Spaceflight. Its payload is also undisclosed.

It has been revealed that finally, at 11:39 p.m. EST on Saturday, SpaceX returns to SLC-4E for USSF-380, another classified Space Force mission. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

Closing out the week on Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the late Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of science and supplies to the ISS.

Last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 5:51 p.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from Taiyuan carrying Shijian-24. China has not said what the satellite does; CGTN reported only that it reached its planned orbit.

On Friday, Nov. 20, at 6:59 a.m. EST, a Long March 8A launched from the commercial launch site at Wenchang with the 30th batch of satellites for Guowang, China’s state-backed broadband megaconstellation.

That night, at 11:20 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-317 mission from Vandenberg, two days later than planned. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.

In a recent development, the week closed on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 7:23 a.m. EST, when a Falcon 9 lifted off from the same pad with the National Reconnaissance Office’s NROL-136, a day later than planned. The launch came 32 hours after USSF-317, SpaceX’s fastest turnaround between launches from the same pad. The booster flew back to Landing Zone 4.

South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD), the military research arm of its defense ministry, is still preparing the first full demonstration flight of its solid-fueled Mir rocket from an offshore platform near Jeju Island. After canceling a June 30 attempt over safety concerns, the ministry has said only that it aims to launch by the end of the year.

It has been revealed that exPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), also has a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan on the books no earlier than November 2026. Its payload has not been announced.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, in 1973, U.S.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, in 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

In a recent development, kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Big Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the problem near and dear to his heart: health care.

Industry observers note that “Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss states. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare aims from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

Industry observers note that the Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

In a recent development, overall, Mitt & Ted gave me newly introduced appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss says. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”.

#88581. A Blind Woman Mastered Echolocation in Just 10 Weeks—And You Can Learn This Superpower Too, Scientists Say

A Blind Woman Mastered Echolocation in Just 10 Weeks—And You Can Learn This Superpower Too, Scientists Say

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Earlier this year, Jayne Hyde-Dryden was walking down a busy sidewalk along a noisy, two-lane road with her friend when she realized just how much her perception had changed.
  • This amazed her friend because Hyde-Dryden is blind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Earlier this year, Jayne Hyde-Dryden was walking down a busy sidewalk along a noisy, two-lane road with her friend when she realized just how much her perception had changed. Mid-conversation, her friend interrupted and noted, “Oh, that was fascinating. You just avoided a van without realizing you’d done it.”.

This amazed her friend because Hyde-Dryden is blind. She had used echolocation to detect the van, which was parked on the sidewalk, and navigated around it without even noticing. “I wasn’t consciously thinking about what I was doing at the time. Instead, I was naturally using echolocation, picking up changes in the way sound reflected from the vehicle and using that information to navigate around the obstacle,” says Hyde-Dryden, a rehabilitation teacher in the UK. Like many blind echolocators, she creates a sharp, quick sound by clicking her tongue and then listens for the echo.

While echolocation comes easily to her now, Hyde-Dryden had to work hard to learn it. Almost 20 years ago, while she was losing her sight to glaucoma, she attended a short workshop and spent hours practicing the clicking technique she learned there. But she didn’t feel confident using it until 2019 when she signed up for an intensive echolocation study at Durham University.

That study was spearheaded by Lore Thaler, PhD, a neuroscientist at Durham University whose work over the last 15 years has uncovered how echolocation changes the brain. Her research goes beyond studying the variability of perception between people, and highlights just how much one person’s perceptual reality can change, even in a short timeframe.

Thaler started her research journey studying visual perception, but her work took an unexpected turn when a collaborator introduced her to a blind echolocator. At the time, she hadn’t heard of human echolocation, but “the way he described the world was very easy to relate to from a sighted person’s perspective,” she says.

Sources indicate that after diving into the literature, Thaler found scattered and disjointed research on echolocation, and “very little was known about the brain basis of it,” she says. “That’s where we came in.”.

She and her collaborators used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to track two blind participants’ brain activity while they listened to recordings of their own echolocation clicks and echoes.

Recent findings suggest that the auditory cortex responded more to echoes than non-echoes in both participants but so did regions of their visual cortex, including areas associated with visual shape perception. Even though this was what she had hoped to find, actually seeing it “was a wonderful surprise,” says Thaler, leading to “a great feeling of discovery.” When she and her team submitted the paper in 2011, the findings were contentious—so contentious that the journal they submitted to asked double the typical number of reviewers to take a look at it. Some thought it was an incredible finding; others thought it was predictable. But in the end, the paper got published, and when it did, it made a huge splash in the neuroscience community.

In a recent development, the project shifted the way Thaler’s collaborators, and later many in the field, thought about the visual cortex. Perhaps the “visual cortex” was a misleading term, some experts thought. Instead, “maybe it’s a thing for processing spatial information,” notes Melvyn Goodale, PhD, a neuroscientist at Western University and Thaler’s collaborator on the project.

According to recent reports, after that first study on echolocation, Thaler was hooked. She introduced an entire lab of her own at Durham University dedicated to human echolocation research. She went on to study how echolocators perceive motion, navigate new spaces, and distinguish between textures like velvet or glass.

By the time Hyde-Dryden made her way to Durham in 2019, Thaler was embarking on her most ambitious project yet: a 10-week echolocation training program for both blind and sighted people.

Sources indicate that each two-hour training session involved a slew of tasks. One involved standing in front of two foam discs and deciding which was larger. Another required participants to navigate through a virtual maze with recorded clicks and echoes. During every session, participants also explored an indoor or outdoor space with the help of Thaler or one of her collaborators to practice echolocating in the real world. Thaler even brought Hyde-Dryden to the Newcastle train station to help her learn the intricacies of echolocating in a busy, loud environment. Over time, Hyde-Dryden built up a mental “library of echo patterns” for familiar objects.

Recent findings suggest that both blind and sighted participants improved substantially at each of these tasks over the course of the 10 weeks. Just as in the initial 2011 paper and many of her follow-up studies, Thaler also wanted to understand brain activity during echolocation. This time, she had participants hop in the MRI machine both before and after learning to echolocate.

Before the study, Hyde-Dryden had heard from an expert blind echolocator that being inside of the MRI would feel tight and uncomfortable, but when she went into the MRI before the echolocation training, it didn’t bother her at all. After the training, however, the MRI felt quite different. “When I went in at the end, I felt horrendous. I felt ill afterwards. I felt really sick. And I think it was because I was more aware.”.

Those fMRI scans revealed that participants’ brains became attuned to echoes, whether or not they were blind. Echoes elicited a larger response in both the auditory cortex and in the primary visual cortex.

Sources indicate that “It paired I think nicely with what we, up to that point, had only been able to show in these expert echolocators,” Thaler states. But it pushed the findings even further, demonstrating that participants don’t need to be blind to have malleable visual cortices. After just 10 weeks of training, the visual cortex becomes attuned to sounds that carry information about space. And other labs have shown that sighted people don’t even need to learn echolocation to retrain their visual cortex; a few days with a blindfold can tune your visual cortex to sound and touch signals it wouldn’t normally process.

Since that training, Hyde-Dryden has started to use echolocation every day. “It really was an absolute game changer for me,” she notes. Thanks to echolocation, when her daughter was young, Hyde-Dryden was able to use both hands to scoop her up from the bath, bringing her into the bedroom without having to hold a cane at the same time. In conjunction with her cane and guide dog, echolocation has made Hyde-Dryden feel much more confident navigating new spaces. Even in busy train stations with high ceilings where the echo can get lost, she can find her way without assistance.

It has been revealed that despite success stories like hers, “it’s not a skill that is widely taught anywhere in the world,” Hyde-Dryden indicates. Echolocation is taught by a small number of people and is sometimes loosely included in rehabilitation curricula, “but it is certainly not given the emphasis that it should.”.

It has been revealed that thaler hopes to change that. She has offered free workshops for years and, this year, she aims to give training sessions to more than 100 rehabilitation professionals at Guide Dogs UK who will then train their hundreds of clients.

According to recent reports, “I think the neuroscience stuff has been a good vehicle to drive home the message ‘this is real, this has to be taken seriously,’” indicates Thaler. “But then to actually go out and do the training and make it useful for people, of course, that’s still another step.”.

In a recent development, nora Bradford is a cognitive scientist and science journalist. During her Ph.D., she investigated metacognition, or “thinking about thinking.” That research echoes throughout her science writing, as she typically covers perception, cognition, and learning across human and non-human animals. You can find her words in Scientific American, National Geographic, Quanta Magazine, and Science News, as well as in video-form on SciShow and PBS Terra. You can also visit her personal website at www.norabradford.com.

It has been revealed that california Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

In a recent development, the race was reshaped by the Golden State’s latest voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she mentioned in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Recent findings suggest that calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

According to recent reports, one incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

It has been revealed that two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

The bright, rapidly rotating star Gamma (γ) Cassiopeiae illuminates two nearby nebula: the reflection nebula IC 59 (below and to the left of the star) and the emission nebula IC 63 (directly below). The latter is sometimes called the Ghost of Cassiopeia. Both lie roughly 550 light-years away, and are slowly being eroded by Gamma’s harsh ultraviolet glow.
