📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, even the best-laid intends can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

“I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

Sources indicate that the work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

Sources indicate that he named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

Industry observers note that “There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” states Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If hypothetical aliens ever search for technosignatures, thousands upon thousands of satellites orbiting Earth should be an obvious sign that intelligent life exists on this planet. The problem is that an alien spacecraft might be better off keeping its distance. As the spiral into dystopia here on Earth continues, there has been growing concern that someone could take out many of those satellites (and the infrastructure they support) with a nuclear weapon. What would happen in the wake of such an attack is a question keeping scientists from sleeping at night.

According to recent reports, when a team of researchers from Princeton and the University of Wisconsin-Madison gauged the theoretical destruction of a nuclear strike in low-Earth orbit, or LEO, the results were grim. There have been over 13,000 satellites at altitudes under 1,242 miles (2,000 km) since early 2026. Many of these fly close together in a region of about 193-232 square miles (500-600 km2), and the use of LEO has only been expanding as the U.S. Department of Defense continues deploying hundreds more for detecting missiles and carrying out military communications, but they have only become more of a target for hostile forces. In an unnerving thought experiment, the researchers worked out the aftermath of detonating a one-megaton nuclear weapon 311 miles (500 kilometers) above the South Atlantic—they found it would easily wipe out about 98% of satellites.

“Radiation-disabled spacecraft remain in orbit but are assumed to lose maneuverability,” they noted in a study recently posted to the preprint server arXiv. “We follow collisions and breakup fragments in altitude bands, retaining mass and allowing fragments to move above and below their birth altitude after a velocity kick. Both intact objects and debris descend under atmospheric drag.”.

According to recent reports, this is not the first time a “what if” like has been batted around, in theory or otherwise. Nuclear paranoia decades ago led to an actual experiment that revealed the potential horrors of detonating something in LEO. On July 9, 1962, the the Starfish Prime test saw a 1.4-megaton bomb detonated in the Pacific, around 400 km above Johnston Atoll. An artificial radiation belt was created by clouds of electrons released from radioactive debris scattered by nuclear fission. It caused severe damage to satellites that were either in outfit at the time or rolled out soon afterward. Radiation continues to be dangerous long after the initial explosion, because spacecraft continue to pass through it as they orbit, experiencing degrading effects that make them more difficult to maneuver. They then end up at increased risk of collision.

The researchers found that the worst effects from a detonation over the South Atlantic would be from exposure to radiation damage, which would disable 25% of the fleet in not even a day. That would rocket to 78% after three days and 98% after a week. Damaged satellites prone to crashing would collide with each other—or scraps of space junk—and gradually shut down services that rely on them. There would be three collisions within 15 days and double that by 30. Smashing spacecraft would also clog LEO with fragments that would put even more satellites at risk, and at least 19 collisions would occur a year after the detonation. Atmospheric drag would reduce the hazard by removing disabled spacecraft orbiting lower, but those at higher altitudes would remain at the highest risk. Disabled satellites would continue to die off.

Starfish Prime was so disastrous that the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed by the U.S. and the Soviet Union a year later. This enforced an outright ban on testing nuclear weapons anywhere but underground, whether it was on the surface, in the atmosphere, or deep in space. Satellites in LEO have multiplied since the 1960s. How long radioactive ions can keep letting electrons loose above the atmosphere is still uncertain, but satellite breakdowns would be staggering. It would take decades to restore the damaged spacecraft and infrastructure.

“Restoring orbital services would require more than replacing the lost spacecraft,” the researchers stated. “New satellites would need to survive the remaining radiation and debris. The prospect of rapid infrastructure loss followed by years of disruption reinforces the need to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.”.

In a recent development, as if leopards and saber-toothed cats weren’t enough, some ancient human relatives probably also had to contend with predators that swooped down from the skies.Adult male baboon remains found in Africa carry telltale signs of raptor predation. The specimens probably weighed about 22 to 26 kilograms in life. That’s twice the size of the largest primates previously known to be preyed upon by a raptor species and on par with some early human ancestors, researchers report November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology. Guarding against aerial predators may have pressured humans’ ancient cousins to form tighter social groups and develop vocal strategies that preceded language, the researchers say.

Biologists discovered the baboon bones among the high sandstone cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in northeastern Chad. These baboons (Papio anubis) have developed unique survival strategies, such as scaling 50-meter cliffs and digging for water and food. They share the plateau with multiple birds of prey, and the researchers have identified one as the most likely baboon hunter: the Verreaux’s eagle (Aquila verreauxii).

Industry observers note that researchers have long studied predation from land carnivores such as substantial cats and crocodiles as a primary driver of behavioral changes in primates, including human ancestors. While a five-kilogram bird like a Verreaux’s eagle taking down a 22-kilogram monkey may seem unlikely, the raptors appear to have developed specialized hunting techniques.

“It’s pretty brutal, but it’s pretty quick,” indicates Cat Hobaiter, a primatologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland. The eagles stab their talons “straight through the eye, straight through the brain, and that’s a very effective control and kill.” The birds may also drag the baboons off the cliffs, a strategy that golden eagles use to hunt large mountain goats and sheep in the Alps. The birds then dismember the prey and carry off pieces to their nests.

Three adult male baboon skulls that Hobaiter and her colleagues studied had clearly visible punctures through the eye sockets. And two specimens also had gashes across the shoulder bones, which appear to have been made by grasping talons. The researchers estimated the weight of the animals based on the size of the head of their femurs, where these upper leg bones attach to the hip.

While the punctures could come from something other than an eagle’s talon, such as a bite or a bullet, the clean circular holes in the skulls match similar damage to smaller monkeys hunted by eagles, Hobaiter notes.

Industry observers note that “I found the evidence pretty compelling,” indicates Scott McGraw, an evolutionary biologist at Ohio State University in Columbus who was not involved with the work. The punctures look “remarkably similar” to injuries in monkeys hunted by the African crowned eagle in the Taï Forest of Côte d’Ivoire, McGraw says.

The eagles also use the landscape to their advantage, hugging cliffs to stay hidden and possibly hunting in pairs, Hobaiter indicates. It’s possible that one eagle could distract the baboons from above while another swoops up from below a cliff to attack, as has been observed against other prey, she says.

While the research team did not witness an eagle attack a baboon, they did observe the monkeys responding to the Verreaux’s eagles’ presence, though not to other raptors in the area.

When the eagles flew down over a ridge, the baboons immediately barked out an alarm call and climbed over the edge of a cliff to safety, Hobaiter indicates.

The eagles’ ability to hunt large primates suggests that raptors may have also hunted ancient human ancestors, Hobaiter notes. In particular, the genus Australopithecus, which lived about 4 million to 2 million years ago and included the famous fossil named Lucy, had similar body sizes to the baboons. A 2.8-million-year-old skull called the Taung child from the species A. africanus even has puncture and scratch marks that McGraw and other researchers argue probably came from a raptor.

According to recent reports, the threat from birds of prey paints a more complete picture of how and why our ancestors developed certain behaviors, such as social grouping to protect younger animals. Primates also use a range of vocal alerts to warn the group of danger. They use different sounds or combinations of sounds for different threats, such as a predator on the ground or in the sky.

“Those first steps towards combining information in different ways to be more specific … would have been a really important precursor [of language],” Hobaiter states.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s crucial that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

In a recent development, “This has never been anything against John Thune,” remarked Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., noted voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

According to recent reports, whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

It has been revealed that moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

Sources indicate that sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides stated.

Recent findings suggest that “It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

In a recent development, that long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that galerina indica looks unassuming.
  • “Although the effects of psiloids and amatoxins in humans are well documented, their natural roles in the environment remain unresolved, with anti-fungivore defense being the leading hypothesis for both compound classes,” Smith and Kunik, who discovered both substances occurring in this species through mass spectrometry, remarked in a study recently published in Current Biology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that magic mushrooms get their magic from psilocybin and psilocin, psychedelic compounds that warp reality and open portals to other realms. They have also been used by Indigenous Mesoamerican and South American peoples for centuries to induce visions. Though it was once thought that mushrooms were either magic or poisonous, there is one newly discovered species that, because of a bizarre turn in evolution, produces both psilocybin and lethal amatoxins, possibly as a defense against being eaten. That’s one trip you never want to take.

It has been revealed that galerina indica looks unassuming. Growing on rotting palm trunks in the humid swamps of Florida, this tiny brown mushroom has no fairytale spots or fantastical colors, so it seems like just another fungus bound to be stepped on. Under its dark cap is a darker reality. Matthew Smith of the University of Florida is the state’s official mycologist, identifying species that could be toxic and regularly consulting with Poison Control, and his team was searching for potentially lethal mushrooms when undergrad researcher Andrew Kunik noticed something strange. While documenting fungi, he found that handling G. indica turned it blue. This often occurs in psychedelic mushrooms. Further investigation found that, despite having this telltale characteristic, the mushroom Kunik had been analyzing had a more sinister kind of magic.

“Although the effects of psiloids and amatoxins in humans are well documented, their natural roles in the environment remain unresolved, with anti-fungivore defense being the leading hypothesis for both compound classes,” Smith and Kunik, who discovered both substances occurring in this species through mass spectrometry, remarked in a study recently published in Current Biology.

Industry observers note that while G. indica did contain psilocybin, it turned out that the ‘shroom also secreted deadly amatoxins. There is no other species of mushroom known for producing both of these substances, and while trippy psiloids have been shown to have possible therapeutic properties, ingesting amatoxins is fatal because these peptides inhibit the enzyme RNA polymerase from creating RNA copies of genes, which leads to organ failure. Fungi are thought to have evolved to produce amatoxins in order to ward off fungivorous creatures such as snails and nematodes. The genes behind production of both psiloids and amatoxins are usually passed down through fungi to their descendants, but the way these genes are acquired is not always so straightforward. Previous studies have suggested they can be horizontally transferred between different fungal species.

According to recent reports, psiloids are known to be synthesized by a cluster of collaborative genes for which evidence of horizontal gene transfer has been found. The same is suspected of amatoxin synthesis, and though there is less evidence for horizontal transfer, it probably began with a fungal donor lineage (which may not have been the same species) that has yet to be identified. Genome analysis has shown that these and other fungal attributes were acquired by genes that were transferred from one species to another growing in the same vicinity. The genus Galerina is already infamous for amatoxins that make many mushrooms within the genus so deadly. How psiloids entered the genus remains a mystery, though just one fateful transfer could have incorporated the genes for amatoxin synthesis into these mushrooms.

What evidence does exist for the transfer of genes that produce psiloids suggests they seeped into a lineage that did not already contain amatoxins, and in a separate evolutionary event, was absorbed by a separate toxic lineage. Kunik’s discovery also revealed how unpredictable fungi can be. The blue pigmentation that is known to be a sign of a magic mushroom comes from psilocin oligomers, molecules linked together from a few repeating structural units, or monomers. Galerina indica has shown that seeing blue does not always mean a mushroom only contains psilocin or psilocybin. While the exact genes that are responsible for amatoxins in this species are still unidentified, and exactly how psiloids evolved in the Galerina genus can only be hypothesized, there is now another thing in Florida more dangerous than alligators.

Recent findings suggest that “G. indica brings together in a single species the biosynthetic systems associated with both ‘magic mushrooms’ and the world’s deadliest poisonous mushrooms,” Kunik and Smith mentioned, “providing a rare natural system for studying how horizontally acquired secondary-metabolite pathways impact organismal fitness.”.

She lurks right outside Newly introduced York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

This Guy Found a Security Camera’s Exact Location Using Only the Sound of Two Planes

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that geoguessr is a widely popular online geography game where players glimpse one still frame from Google Street View and then attempt to pinpoint the exact location on a world map.
  • Mind you, this audio doesn’t have any useful hints.
  • Industry observers note that to start his journey toward pinpointing the location of this video, with the only limitation being it was filmed somewhere in the continental U.S., the YouTuber first turned to Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast data, or ADS-B, provided by aircraft equipment that constantly report speed, velocity, and altitude.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that geoguessr is a widely popular online geography game where players glimpse one still frame from Google Street View and then attempt to pinpoint the exact location on a world map. Many things can be helpful hints—the design of road signs, the format of license plates, specific road markings as well as surrounding trees and landscapes. However, a YouTuber named colsto took this idea to a whole new level by geolocating an incredibly grainy video by just its captured audio.

Mind you, this audio doesn’t have any useful hints. No one nearby is talking about this “da Bears” game with a thick Chicago accent, for example. But buried within the security camera’s spectrogram (visual display of frequencies over time) is a clue—two of them, in fact. To the uninitiated they look relatively innocuous two sloping lights roughly 920 seconds apart, but colsto recognized these lines as the Doppler effect signatures of a two planes passing overhead.

Industry observers note that to start his journey toward pinpointing the location of this video, with the only limitation being it was filmed somewhere in the continental U.S., the YouTuber first turned to Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast data, or ADS-B, provided by aircraft equipment that constantly report speed, velocity, and altitude. Websites like Flightradar24 rely on this data to provide a real-time snapshot of on-going flights around the world. Colsto first cross-referenced this data and winnowed potential candidates by choosing parameters featuring two planes the right speed and the right distance away while still traveling within 920 seconds of each other. The results weren’t promising.

“That gave us…roughly 70,000 points,” colsto notes in the video. “Now, adding on to all that logic, the silence filter—where that point doesn’t hear another flight between the two events—drops from 70,000 to 15,000. Even with all those constraints, there is just so much land area and so many flights that 15,000 points still meet all those criteria.”.

Instead of going through each data point, ruling out why it doesn’t fit and refining the search parameters, colsto returned to the Doppler curves and revised one of the search’s original assumptions. These two curves didn’t represent a perfect Doppler curve because planes are constantly adjusting speed and heading, and that information—no matter how slight—is locked away within these two curves. So colsto modeled the Doppler curves to create a flight path that could then be checked against 15,000 possible points.

“The Doppler curve is a function of the radial velocity of the plane with respect to the observer,” colsto claims in the video. “The Doppler curve would change depending on the plane geometry.”.

Eventually, colsto found the exact security camera located in Oyster Bay in Long Island, Latest York, that captured the grainy security footage of the pixelated tree line.

According to recent reports, “I’m trying to fear monger with this video. The odds that someone can and does actually do this is pretty slim,” colsto said at the video’s conclusion. “In reality, there’s probably one hundred easier ways to find you than this.”.

That isn’t immensely reassuring.

Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday.
  • President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.
  • Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., stated that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

It has been revealed that “Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

Sources indicate that the nomination of Thumann Severs, who right now serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

At the moment Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Recent findings suggest that sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., mentioned Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”.

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC right now focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Recent findings suggest that committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he mentioned Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places crucial limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz noted. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”.

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

Industry observers note that however, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

“Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she remarked. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”.

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs mentioned she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”.

Luján also asked Thumann Severs to name complications where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she remarked her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

It has been revealed that thumann Severs said that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it right now exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

Industry observers note that “Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any newly introduced Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”.

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been declared by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

Latest Update: This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was presently looking at.
  • “Right when I got home from the hospitals, I was seeing my cat in my mother and my sister,” states the 29-year-old teacher, who has asked to go by Karl to protect his privacy.
  • Sources indicate that it was unsettling, to say the least.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was presently looking at. To his bewilderment, the swapping of features even extended to his pet cat Luna.

“Right when I got home from the hospitals, I was seeing my cat in my mother and my sister,” states the 29-year-old teacher, who has asked to go by Karl to protect his privacy. “That was one of the first things that I noticed,” he says. “And the cat even took on resemblances of people.”.

Sources indicate that it was unsettling, to say the least. “Looking at her and then looking at somebody else, I might see her giant eyes on a person.”.

Scientists have now described Karl’s perception of faces in the December glitch of Cortex. His condition, in which echoes of a previously viewed image appear in a new context, is called palinopsia, and it was likely caused by Karl’s brain surgery. Because the echoes appear on faces, they distort how faces look to him, a condition known as prosopometamorphopsia. The new work offers clues about how brains perceive faces, both under normal and unusual conditions.

According to recent reports, the researchers’ analyses of the man’s face perceptions are “wonderfully innovative,” claims clinical psychiatrist Jan Dirk Blom of Leiden University and Parnassia Psychiatric Institute in the Netherlands, who was not involved in the work. “In this era of big data and complex statistical analyses, we almost forget how informative clinical observations in single patients can be.”.

Karl’s unusual perceptions caught the attention of researchers. “His face processing system is disrupted, and it’s disrupted in a specific way,” says Brad Duchaine, a visual neuroscientist at Dartmouth University. “For reasons we don’t understand, items from memory are being pulled up and pasted onto the face that he’s perceiving.”.

Duchaine’s lab has been collecting case studies of people who perceive faces differently in an effort to learn about visual perception. Duchaine and his colleagues assessed Karl’s experiences by showing him images of faces and asking him to describe what he saw. This confirmed that he consistently saw distortions in the eye regions of faces, such as the shape, and in faces’ shading and sometimes even texture. As they worked together, Duchaine and Karl used AI-image generators to create pictures of faces that resemble what Karl saw for the cat-human swap.

Karl isn’t the only person with palinopsia that affects faces, Duchaine says. A few other people have contacted him who also see echoes of prior faces. But Karl’s palinopsia seems different. “His were really consistent, very long-lasting. And then the cross-species transfer is something that I’d never heard before,” with one major exception, Duchaine says. A case study from 1986 describes a woman who, after seeing a poodle on a bus, saw poodle heads on every other passenger, too. That woman’s distortions lasted only about half an hour; Karl’s perceptual shifts have been consistently present since his 2024 surgery.

Industry observers note that “What is new about the present study is the finding that a cat’s eyes can apparently be transposed from memory banks onto human faces observed in the here and now, and vice versa,” notes Blom. “And that we now have a rough idea of the brain areas making this possible.”.

During a surgery to correct malformed blood vessels, doctors removed tissue from Karl’s right posterior temporal area, a part of the brain known to be involved in face recognition. Karl’s experiences hint at how the visual system detects and interprets features on faces, Duchaine states. There’s an idea that humans interpret faces holistically, as a single object, he says. Karl’s case shows some of the limits of this idea, because he’s having these effects specific to the eye region, Duchaine says.

“It’s sort of like a filter,” Karl notes, describing his experience of palinopsia. “It decides on a style, and then that style is applied to everyone in my reality, including myself.” These filters can change across a day or last several weeks, Karl says. He’s even experienced eye feature swaps from a face he saw in a dream. “And that was then applied to me, looking in a mirror, and then everybody else.”Karl also experiences echoes of environments, he says. For instance, if he has visited an area with lots of potholes in the roads, visual echoes of those potholes can appear in a newer road. A similar thing can happen with shapes, he says: Echoes of square hallways or stairwells can appear in newly introduced spots.

Sources indicate that using AI and collaboration to help re-create what Karl sees is an advance, Blom says. And this sort of collaboration between scientist and volunteer is crucial. “In my line of work, clinical psychiatry, we know that everything stands and falls with the descriptions that our patients give us,” he says. “In my opinion, this is patient participation at its best.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that more Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete blueprint” that provides change.

In a recent development, “I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”.

Sanders noted during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a upcoming and bold direction.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”.

Sources indicate that “Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”.

Sources indicate that some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking remarked he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”.

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but stated she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she noted, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”.

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”.

Asked about his prepares Monday evening, Van Hollen noted, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”.

According to recent reports, “What I’ve mentioned from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”.

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he stated of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

According to recent reports, “That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she mentioned.

It has been revealed that gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is presently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., stated he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”.

Industry observers note that sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., mentioned Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”.

In a recent development, “Yes,” he said of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”.

“And we can do that with Chuck Schumer.”.

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, some toys are timeless. From monster trucks that power over boulders to speed demons that clock 70 miles per hour, RC cars can thrill anyone who gets a controller in their hand for hours on end. Whether you’re an experienced driver looking to splurge on a higher-end model, a beginner looking for a newly introduced hobby, or a parent just trying to get your kid off the iPad, remote control cars are a great toy for all ages.

Sources indicate that if you’re fresh to the RC world, shopping for a car (or an RC airplane, boat, or truck, for that matter) may feel somewhat daunting at first. It can get surprisingly technical, especially if you're looking at the hobby-grade cars. It helps to, at the very least, know how to tell the difference between the cars made for competitive racing and off-roading, detail-oriented models for collectors, and the more affordable options for kids and beginners. The good news is that while there may be a bit of a learning curve, you can get a taste of the action no matter your budget.

For more great toys kids of all ages are sure to love, check out our picks for the best remote control toys, the best drones, and the best robot toys.

Our testing focused on key features that factor into an RC car's day-to-day use, including speed, power, battery life, and handling. We drove a collection of cars on both flat indoor surfaces in our office, over uneven, hilly outdoor areas in Upcoming York’s Central Park, and through the fall foliage and around a tree-lined backyard in upstate New York. In addition to the basics, we measured the cars' acceleration, how promptly each car responded to radio signals, and checked the range of the remotes. We also took general notes on how easy it was to get the cars up and running.

Sources indicate that there are two models on this list we haven't tested: the Bezgar Off-Road Monster Truck and the Tamiya Nismo R34 GT-R Z-Tune. We recommended them after reviewing user recommendations and enthusiast reviews to find cars that represented certain areas our test units didn't fill. Our research spanned a range of different vehicle types from reputable RC brands, including Traxxas, Laegendary, Redcat Racing, and Bezgar.

According to recent reports, across the board, we wanted to make sure this list represented a wide range of RC cars, including options at several price points. Our picks include toy cars that cost $50 or less, mid-range RC cars under $200, and a few pricey models for experienced adult enthusiasts that cost as much as $350.

According to recent reports, in our latest update, we performed additional testing on our existing recommendations, as well as a few fresh cars. We also removed one recommendation, the VR Real Racer, as it has been out of stock for several months.

According to recent reports, the Traxxas Stampede RC car is our top choice because it combines speed, handling, and power better than any other option we tested. Its oversized monster truck tires aren’t just for show: They provided great traction and grip on dirt and rocks, as well as concrete and linoleum. Even compared to more speed-focused cars, the Traxxas brings some notable zip.

Industry observers note that what impressed us most, though, was the handling. Even on uneven grass and dirt, we felt comfortable making sharp turns and precise movements at high speeds and the vehicle didn’t topple over. And it handled crashes like a champ: It took a few accidental head-on collisions into trees and fell as much as three feet off some rocks in the park and was no worse for wear.

In a recent development, another key distinction for this RC car was how responsive and powerful the suspension was. Driving on bumpy surfaces and through dirt never swayed or threw it off course. The suspension made it easier to perform short jumps over ramps and ledges without crashing or damaging the vehicle.

Sources indicate that this well-priced off-road monster truck has working roll bar headlights, a spare tire attached to the back chassis, and an aluminum body that handles collisions at the truck’s top speed of 12 miles per hour. Its feature-rich design is an excellent value for beginners and experienced RCers alike.

Sources indicate that the two-wheel-drive remote-control car is on the smaller side, at 1/14th scale, but it has a powerful motor to keep it rolling for up to 20 minutes on its all-terrain tires. The 2.4 GHz remote works from a distance of more than 160 feet away.

While it isn't quite as powerful or durable as our top pick, it serves as a perfect on-ramp to hobby-grade RC, giving you more oomph than a cheap toy.

If you’ve got a love for model cars, this is the right RC car for you. This scaled-down Ford Bronco is the near spitting image of the real thing, minus the less-than-ideal gas mileage. This miniature has grippy tires that match its slow but powerful motor. Just like the real thing, this Bronco climbs over rocks and rallies up inclines with ease.

We tested the car going up large boulders in the park, and while it never zoomed over them, it continued moving effortlessly. We, of course, love the accurate exterior shell, but also found the interior body to be quite impressive.

According to recent reports, the TRX-4M has a flexible frame and suspension system that allows for easy climbing on uneven surfaces. It comes with two headlights which, when the Bronco shell is snapped on, only further adds to the look.

You can grab one of these RC cars in multiple colors, including blue, orange, white, red, and black.

If you want speed, try out this LaTrax Desert Prerunner racing truck. While it may not win you any competitive RC races with professional builds, this is a hobby-grade car with some serious juice behind it for its size. Driving it around required a bit of adjustment time because of its quick acceleration and sharp turning radius, but that’s exactly the type of challenge we love to tackle.

The grippy tires and bouncy suspension also meant that this car picks up some serious speed outdoors. We drove it over hills and through rocks without losing any speed in the process. We loved the way it spins and drifts when it has some dirt or gravel underneath it and found ourselves trying to spin it around trees for fun.

Sources indicate that the car, much like other Traxxas products, is also quite durable. It handled a few spills and wipeouts with no real damage to the body or motor. That said, be careful driving it through leaves and sticks because we found several accumulated under the outer shell after our drive.

Sources indicate that many of the RC cars we tested are off-roaders with thick tires, grippy treads, and bouncy suspensions. This allows them to drive quickly and responsively across tons of different surfaces like dirt, gravel, grass, and up rocks. This model from Tamiya is designed for the exact opposite: It features slick, smooth tires and a low-profile design that's built for outdoor or indoor play on hard surfaces like tile or hardwood.

According to recent reports, this is because the remote control car is built for one thing and one thing only: drifting. Just like stunt drivers on a movie set, these cars spin and slide across the ground for cinematic turns and stylish maneuvering.

Recent findings suggest that bear in mind, however, that this car does not come ready to race. This is an assembly kit that requires patience, steady hands, and additional materials like glue and a hobby knife. Furthermore, the car will also require an electronic speed controller (ESC), battery, and radio receiver.

Recent findings suggest that if you aren't ready to commit to full-size model, this tiny RC car from Hot Wheels fits in the palm of your hand, and has an equally miniature price tag. While it doesn't have the speed or torque of the larger models on this list, this is a perfect way to introduce young kids to the thrill of remote control driving.

The mini Lambo, a 1/16th scale model, is also perfect gift for sports car lovers looking for a bit of fun. The RC car is built with a rechargeable battery already in the body. So, whenever it needs to be charged up, plug the cable directly into the car.

According to recent reports, the mini size is more for just convenience, too. The car is designed to fit and drive on all the same Hot Wheels tracks that work for the classic die cast models the brand is known for. So, if you already have a Hot Wheels enthusiast in mind, this is a great addition to their collection.

Based on our testing, the biggest distinction between RC cars is that some are hobby-grade models for racing or off-roading hobbyists, and others are beginner-friendly toys that are usually made for kids and beginners.

Hobby-grade RC cars come with powerful motors, beefy batteries, and the torque and speed to handle outdoor driving over tough terrain or competitive racing. These are typically more expensive than their toy counterparts and are better suited for buyers who want to seriously dive into RC cars or are already major fans. Toy RC cars are slower and get less run time per charge, but are much more affordable.

It has been revealed that RC cars also come in a wide variety of builds, including off-road 4x4s and buggies, rock crawlers (built for more rigid, extreme off-roading), and drift cars (best for turns and speed). You’ll often see the RC car’s scale listed, especially for model cars, representing its size in relation to the real deal.

While shopping, you may see the initials “RTR” in product descriptions, which stand for “ready to race.” This means you can start driving right out of the box or after charging, with no extra parts required to get it up and running. Cars may be labeled RTR even if the batteries are sold separately, though, so make sure to check the packaging.

Sources indicate that speed varies depending on what the car is built to do. For example, rock climbers don’t have to be incredibly fast to tackle boulders, but they need powerful high-torque motors, whereas a race car should hit at least 20 to 30 miles per hour, depending on your level of competition. Before you buy, make sure you have in mind where you expect most of your RC driving to happen and what kind of features are important to you.

If you want a taste of everything, there are a number of cars that are in the middle ground, offering enough speed to make straightaways fun and enough power to handle grass, inclines, and some gravel.

Less expensive RC cars generally have a two-button remote control, and those on the higher end have 2.4 GHz (a speedy signal transmission speed) pistol-grip-style remotes with more advanced steering and throttles. These remotes are more responsive, allowing you to make quick turns, rapidly accelerate, or even reverse at a moment's notice. 2.4 GHz remote controls are what you’ll likely see in any hobby-grade RC cars. If you go for a high-end model, ensure that replacement parts and upgrades are readily available. Otherwise, you’ll have to search for outdated parts on eBay.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle.
  • Industry observers note that house and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen.
  • In their latest positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Industry observers note that house and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their latest positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

Industry observers note that republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

Moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so key,” the Ohio senator stated in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his new role as “a hell of a job.” He said Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”.

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

Moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is at the moment serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

According to recent reports, brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored substantial wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

In an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”.

Industry observers note that the 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

Recent findings suggest that on the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

House Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that we’re constantly testing and writing about pocket knives here at Popular Mechanics, and Benchmade is a brand that always tops our list of favorites. Its folders, automatics, flippers, and fixed blades are beautifully designed using all high-quality materials, and all are U.S.-made in its Oregon headquarters. But there’s no denying they’re pricey, costing upward of $200, and they rarely go on sale for much of a discount.

But right now, ahead of Black Friday, Benchmade is knocking 20 percent off three of its most popular knives on Amazon—the Osborne, the Bugout, and the Bailout—for a savings of roughly $70 each.

Industry observers note that when the Osborne debuted in 2000, it was Benchmade’s first blade to sport the Axis lock, which been replicated in some form by nearly every major knife manufacturer since its patent expired in 2019. It’s designed for ambidextrous operation and fast, one-handed deployment, plus it keeps your fingers clear of the blade while you open and close the knife.

Recent findings suggest that this seasonal version uses CPM-S90V stainless super steel, which offers great edge retention and reliable toughness for everyday tasks like opening boxes. It’s coated with a protective distressed finish to make the reverse tanto-style blade look rustic and has a rich-looking dark-green aluminum handle, with copper accents. It feels good in hand—a durable yet lightweight EDC knife.

The Bugout is the knife our resident expert Justin Park grabs first for backpacking, camping and hunting and says it’s “arguably the defining pocket knife of the explosion of modern EDC blades.” It’s strong, but ultra lightweight and hardly registers in your pocket or pack.

Like the Osborne above, the Bugout uses S90V stainless super steel, featuring a shorter drop-point blade, copper accents, and handle that combines the same dark-green aluminum with a grippy and rugged-looking canvas micarta.

The Bailout is lightweight and tough. It has a longer drop-point tanto-style S90V stainless steel blade covered in the same stonewashed protective finish as the Bugout and Osborne, along with the same dark-green aluminum handle and copper accents. While it’s another great choice for EDC, the Bailout is outfitted with tactical-style elements, like the lanyard slot at the rear and the deep-carry clip.

Independents decide the election, again!

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of newly introduced senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E.
  • It has been revealed that once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep.
  • “We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of newly introduced senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

It has been revealed that once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Recent findings suggest that independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they demonstrated up.

It has been revealed that looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

It has been revealed that for example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

Despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

According to recent reports, overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Recent findings suggest that clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

In the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top glitch concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent remarked it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

It has been revealed that the president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent mentioned his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

In a recent development, trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic issues and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls demonstrated that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

It has been revealed that at a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent remarked the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

Marella Cruises‘ Discovery 2 is currently undergoing enhancements in a wet dock in Málaga, Spain.

According to a recent social media patch, the 1995-built vessel is being prepared to become an adults-only vessel, in addition to undergoing routine maintenance.

The former Legend of the Seas will undergo engine work and main pool retiling, with the Glass House Pool getting a fresh coat of paint and the atrium fresh seating, complete with a refreshed Snack Shack.

The ship is set to welcome only adults starting in 2027 with former youth facilities transformed into four new venues, including Marella’s first private karaoke lounge.

Amplify Karaoke will operate as a private lounge for up to seven guests, which can be booked by the hour.

Other new venues include the Lost Luggage Bureau, a speakeasy venue inspired by the Golden Age of Travel, allowing passengers to take part in two 90-minute reveals that include live music, live actors, storytelling and three signature cocktails.

The Marella Discovery 2 will also introduce Red Handed, an escape room set backstage at the fictional Cabaret Rouge in the 1920s, where teams of up to six guests have 60 minutes to steal Lady Ruby Bardot’s diamond necklace before they’re caught red-handed.

Also being added is The Loft, which is described as a calm space for passengers who want to slow down, combining a library, board games, and hosted arts and crafts in a relaxed setting.

Following the enhancements in wet dock, the Marella Discovery 2 is scheduled to operate a winter season in the Canaries and Madeira, offering seven-night cruises from Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Puerto del Rosario to destinations in Spain and Portugal.
